text:
Still not good value even on PCIe 4.0 11 months later. An RX 6600 can be had for ~150-160%+ of the price of an RX 6500XT in most regions, has multiple times the performance (it's not even a contest). And that's just the raw rendering power. Its 8GB ensures that it will last a good while longer, whilst 4GB was built into entry-level Full-HD cards six years ago already for reason. And that's just gaming  -- the 6500XT is basically a laptop chip with no features or extras whatsoever.

On the high end, both AMD and Nvidia factor in that price doesn't matter at all. So they charge up to a ridiculous 2,000 bucks for a GPU. Just as on a Ferrari car, for the customers, it doesn't matter. They want the fastest thing on the market. On the lower end meanwhile, they know that price is the ONLY thing that matters. As a result, the best bang for the buck can be always had in different tiers.

Additionally, pairing 4GB of VRAM with but 4 PCIe lanes has been the second most anti-consumer practice on the GPU market this year considering how recent PCIe 4.0 is -- alongside Nvidia's more recently released RTX 3060 8GB, which performs more like a RTX 3050ti. Still better than nothing, I guess. :-)

Purchased 2 of those from Asus for 180€ each for my nephew's for Xmas. 
They don't have a top notch PC anyways so a high end gpu  would be overkill. And while the feature set is a bit annoying, 64bit memory bandwidth and pice X4 all should be fine for what it will be used for (Fortnite, Forza horizon, fifa) as long as they stay within the VRAM limit.

Buying used was no option on a gift, for more then one reason: 
1 they are new
2 warranty
3 and a guarantee you don't end up with a miner card that is on it's dying bed and will go in couple of months. (The miner pandemic was one major reason to not even look at used cards anymore)

The other option I looked at was one of those Rx 580 sp2048 from various Chinese brands, but once again it's a bit of a gamble imo and probably a pain in the rear if you have to return it. 

I needed something reliable, from a brand i trust so I can slap them in, install drivers and won't hear about any issues in a few weeks.

For myself i would have probably gone with a Chinese Rx 580 so 2048 cause it was even cheaper. 

And honestly the cut features on the Rx 6500 XT don't bother me that much as the fps are still good enough regardless. I'd say on par with a good old Rx 580 (the real one). 4gb VRAM however is minimum in 2022 but totally fine given the GPUs performance. Medium to high settings should be good.

Sure one of my nephew's is going to be a bit disappointed as he wants to play Fortnite on max settings and wanted a rtx 3080 for Christmas but he has to deal with it. Surely not going to buy a 10 years old a 1000 bucks gpu (+ new case + new power supply as the card wouldn't even fit and the 500w power supply would hardly do). text:
It's pretty onpar with the 1650 Super (and a lot of the time a GTX 1060). I still don't consider the 6500XT to be any really good value. It's a low end and budget product, alright. That is "budget" in today's market of inflated GPU prices, of course.

But similar to the high end market, where prices don't matter at all -- this is a product where price is the only thing that matters. Just a tier above the value you get is so much better it's not a contest. I'm looking for a possible replacement for my aging 1050ti, but this is not going to be it. The 1050ti as entry-level to 1080p gaming was paired with 4GB of VRAM 6 years ago already. As a result, it can actually still game quite a few AAA games with ~45fps medium settings such as Elden Ring half a decade later.

The 6500XT meanwhile won't offer anywhere near that value as even on lower settings and older games on higher settings, the 4GB are just about enough. And that's just the VRAM. The advantage in rendering power on a RX6600 is much higher than any of the benchmarks in this video suggests. So you can keep it even after a CPU upgrade or with your next system some more.

"Cheap" means "cheap" in this case.

text:
In a world where a huge part of gaming culture is streaming and content creation...releasing a card with no hardware video encoding is bad.

Which could be saved by using an APU for hardware video encoding.

Oh, wait. The APUs AMD currently has released are PCIe 3.0, and this only has 4 lanes. So you're heavily bandwidth limited, and that means that pushing the framebuffer over the PCIe to the APU will absolutely impact performance.

No content creator or streamer can justify this card. And that makes it pretty much dead on arrival.

author: @TheWorldEndsWithUs

text:
The 6500XT unfortunately has too many flaws for me to recommend right now. 
Pretty weak to no performance gains over its predecessors (RX570, RX580, GTX 1060, GTX 1660 and similar performance bracket cards) which means that anyone who has anything similar or better, there is no point getting it for rasterisation
Ray Tracing for AMD cards as of current are weaker than their RTX counterparts, and with a 4GB VRAM buffer and clearly worse performance than the RTX 3050, even FSR couldn't help with those issues. The latter GPU also supports DLSS which in my personal experience, can keep good image quality for performance boosts whilst aiming for 1660 Ti performance where as the 6500XT falls short of that in many cases.
4GB VRAM as mentioned above. Great for an Entry Level GPU, but one aimed as a budget mainstream option for the masses, not worth it in 2022
Missing Video encode and decode instructions, meaning it's not friendly to content creators. Not important for ones who'd buy the latest and greatest but for budget minded users, it's at a huge disadvantage.
PCIe x4. The 6600 and 6600XT suffered minimal to minor performance loss when going from PCIe 4.0 to 3.0, which the latter you can expect a great deal many gamers are still on. The 6500XT has been demonstrated to have noticeable to MAJOR drops when doing that same move. Arguments in using RESIZE or BAR is irrelevant if many people holding out on older legacy systems.
The only saving grace, damned by faint praise it be, is that I can actually find a stock of them in the UK for £200 starting prices, making it slightly easier to swallow in price versus the GTX 1050 Ti and 1650 which are the closest priced cards for it. But that's not me endorsing the fact that there was a time I can get an RX 570 for £120.
If the RTX 3050 can maintain close to MSRP (which may be difficult in the US but in the UK, so far some cards held decent prices. If it sold for £250-300, I'd still recommend it over the 6500XT), I'd even go as far to cautiously recommend it over the 6500XT in every way. Cautious is the word is because I rather it be at MSRP or even less because for such performance we had years back, we shouldn't be spending this much. 

TL;DR: 6500XT is not a product I can recommend.

text:
Excellent video, it seems you're one of the few tech youtubers to speak logically about this GPU. What people aren't mentioning is the fact that online retailers or stores like Best Buy/Micro Center are still selling GTX 1050 ti's for $259.99 or worse yet, GT 1030's for $130.00. That is the true crime against PC gamers. The fact that someone with limited information on PC's could go out and drop almost $300 on a budget ($139) card from 2016 in 2022 is way more unacceptable than AMD releasing this card. 

Performance wise, this is basically on par with a GTX 1060 6GB, GTX 1650 Super, or to a RX 580 like you mentioned. On ebay each of those mentioned cards are still averaging a $275 - $320 selling price. The fact is, countless people trying to get into PC gaming have had to settle on used cards like that for the past year+, used aging cards that could fail at any time and leave them with a paper weight.

So like you mentioned, this is not a card for someone who wants to upgrade their GTX 1080 ti to a new powerhouse and I understand the immense frustration those people have (myself included) to not be able to walk into a store and purchase a RTX 3070 or similar at MSRP. But a huge factor that shouldn't go unnoted is the fact that this is at least helping to fill a void, the people who want someone new that will run new games at reasonable settings who have been shit out of luck for over a year.

Naturally this and other new budget GPUs like the soon to be released RTX 3050 will help significantly drive down the prices of comparable older GPUs on the used marketplace (Ebay, FB Marketplace, Craigslist) that are still capable of low 1080p gaming (GTX 1070, 1650 super, 1060, / RX 580, 480) which in effect will finally make those true budget cards again and not $270+ on ebay which helps justify  people selling RTX 3060's for $800. 

It's all relative and I see this card being very successful and I would unequivocally recommend this GPU to anyone over going for a used GTX 1070 for $350 that someone probably "fixed" with their moms hair dryer.

text:
AMD has supported PCIE 4.0 for 3 years now. You can get a PCIE 4.0 motherboard for $50.

What a lot of people don't seem to understand is that it was this card or no card. This is a upclocked laptop die slapped on a PCB for use in desktop. There was originally no intention of selling this die on desktop. This decision was made after tape out. Adding more lanes and encoders would have meant a new die. The lead time on a new die is 10 months and the cost of a new die is around 200 million USD on 7nm.

Its not like Nvidia is offering any alternatives at this price point. What are you going to buy? A 1650? That card is significantly weaker on a PCIE 4.0 motherboard.

text:
@gamingcyber334  Yes, a lot of people are still happily on Kaby Lake and earlier, but most are upgrading to the newest platforms available via bundles and sales. The "some people" are an exception but the majority are able to upgrade, even if it's slowly. DDR4 RAM (2x8gb kit) has been affordable due to DDR5, as low as $50 from retail (Crucial has been dumping a lot recently in waves for instance). CPUs, at the moment the i5-12600K is $295 - 300 across most retailers and it's going to go lower once the next generation is ready for release. The AMD Ryzen 5 5600X is also roughly around the same pricing and it will expect the same outcome. As for motherboards, they of course can vary but the ones that fit most people's needs are less that $150.

If one is going for Intel, they have to make sure they can get a DDR4 supported motherboard due to DDR5 price to performance currently. Cheapest B560 that supports DDR4 from retail is the Asus PRIME B660M-A D4, can be had for $140 right now from Amazon and it should meet a gamer's needs. If going for AMD, the cheapest B550 from retail is the ASRock B550M-HDV for $80 from Newegg, and it'll meet a budget gamer's needs just fine. Both Intel and AMD routes will be roughly $450 - 500 at the moment regardless which ever is taken (taking into account CPU + Mobo). And, deals will always happen for other alternatives and other components.

As for the GPU... I would not consider the RX 6500XT at its current price, save some money and get the RX 6600 or RX 6600XT since they are more often in stock, but I imagine it will go down to lower than $150 since nobody wants to buy this junk due to its price to performance and other negative compromises. Miners might play with it to see how much hashrates they can get but won't depend on it and will not recommend usage of it, scalpers will try to flip them because "shiny GPU" for a month or two but since nobody wants to buy them at even higher pricing they will sell them at the price they bought it for (or even less), and most gamers won't buy it because their eyes are not on a card like this. They want a GPU such as the RTX 3060 or RX 6600 minimum, which those go for at least $500 retail (pretty sure the 3060 goes for a few hundred more). Only the budget gamers will consider this card over other options, but give it some time and this will be at a great price anyways. Just take a look at the Ryzen 7 5800X, while it didn't receive as much harsh criticism from reviewers and consumers (because it wasn't a bad chip) it was the first Ryzen 5000 chip to be regularly in stock and the first to begin having its price slashed closer to what many said it should've been (I bought mine at $440 since it was the only in stock option at the time and it's currently regularly available at $360, close to the price many said it should've been at in the first place).

Am I still missing some point? Once again I understand a lot of people cannot upgrade due to financial reasons so they're stuck with a DDR3-supported machine but there's even more people looking to upgrade everything anyway. From what I've read, a lot of people looking for a low budget gaming GPU in countries with unfortunate financial circumstances do appreciate this GPU due to it actually being affordable for them, and we'll just have to wait and see what the 3050 will do (I imagine it will be better performing but more expensive, out of stock regularly, and scalped to shit like every other GPU, as well as the Intel GPUs that are upcoming but really we'll just have to wait and see).

text:
I like and respect Zach very, very much. That being said, I don't think I could disagree any more strongly.
I do NOT lay any of the blame on Zach regarding any part of the craziness that has taken over the entire GPU market in the last couple of years, but I do think that opinions like his may be propagating, and even proving the effectiveness of, an enormous marketing push across the entire market to gaslight the average consumer into expecting that they should have to pay way more money for way less performance than what current gen tech is able to deliver.
I think it's somewhat dangerous, on the consumer level, once we get to the point where we look at what the 6500XT is and how it performs (as well as any other card to come out in the last two year compared to its market price) and we begin to accept that as 'normal' and as 'just the way it is'.
People with enough disposable income that buying the newest or biggest of everything is easy for them is one thing, but the boom in crypto prices is the exception, not the rule. That and all of the other supply/demand variables that have come into play to create the perfect storm for GPU pricing. Those values as well as the GPU prices that go up and down along with them as long as there are suckers who continue buying in, will ALWAYS rise and fall as long as GPUs are able to mine with. But if GPU manufacturers/distributors truly have their way, they will convince as many people as possible that less performance for more money is how it's 'supposed to be'. That way they can just drive prices way up on ALL GPUs, ALL of the time and make those huge, inflated profits ALL of the time and not just when crypto is up and there are new cards released

The name and specs are the only things that we have at our disposal to signal the intent of a product. The negative reviews come from a mismatch of the reviewers expectations with reality. text:
I think the biggest issue with this card is how severely it was cut down. Yes, AMD is a business looking to profit at all times, and yes, more features would make this card more appealing to miners, but at this stage, the feature set is stripped down to a point where this card is a close competitor with a 5 year old product at the same "price" (depends strongly on the prices this and the RX580 are in your region).

I think a better way to sell this product would be to call it the RX6500 (leave room for an XT variant that is more competitive when GPU prices continue to come down), give it a PCI-e x8 bus, and put the encoding and decoding capabilities back in. Leaving it with 4GB of VRAM is honestly for the best, considering that anything over that puts it in the miners' sphere of interest, but every other shortcoming makes it a very bitter pill to swallow, especially considering that 200$ is an absolute best case scenario. But again, businesses gonna business, and consumers gonna consume for as long as the market is the way it is.
